item.title: Non-defining relative clauses: adding extra information
item.explanation_text: A non-defining relative clause adds extra information about a noun that is already clear. It is separated by commas: My sister, who lives in Seoul, is a nurse. Use who for people, which for things, whose for possession, where for places and when for times. In a non-defining clause you cannot use that, and you cannot leave the relative pronoun out. which can also refer back to a whole idea: He passed the exam, which surprised everyone. A defining clause has no commas, because it tells us which person or thing we mean: The man who called you is my uncle.
item.contrast_text: Compare: My brother who works in IT lives in Tashkent (I have more than one brother; this tells you which one). My brother, who works in IT, lives in Tashkent (I have one brother; his job is extra information).
item.common_error_pattern: Using that after a comma, joining two sentences with only a comma ('..., it was...'), or leaving out the commas around extra information.

examples.bad: Samarkand, that is over 2,500 years old, attracts many tourists.
examples.good: Samarkand, which is over 2,500 years old, attracts many tourists.

examples.bad: The train was late, what meant we missed the meeting.
examples.good: The train was late, which meant we missed the meeting.

examples.bad: Dilnoza, her brother is my classmate, is coming tonight.
examples.good: Dilnoza, whose brother is my classmate, is coming tonight.

examples.bad: We spent a day in Bukhara, there we saw the Ark fortress.
examples.good: We spent a day in Bukhara, where we saw the Ark fortress.
